name: Sweet potato / carb timing

card.summary: Scheduling carbs like sweet potato around workouts; the timing effect itself is debated.

quick.overview:
Carb timing is the practice of eating carbohydrates such as sweet potato at set times around training.

The "anabolic window" idea is presented as a suggestion rather than established, and sweet potato has not been studied specifically.
quick.mechanism: Carbohydrates replenish muscle glycogen used in high-intensity exercise, which proponents say speeds recovery.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented for this practice beyond general dietary considerations.

lead: Sweet potato carb timing is the practice of scheduling carbohydrate-rich meals, often built around sweet potato, near training sessions so that workouts are fuelled and muscle glycogen is restored afterwards. Lifters and bodybuilders use it to train harder and recover faster, which over time supports more muscle and a leaner, more athletic physique.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes nutrient timing as coordinating food intake with exercise, with carbohydrate during and after workouts said to replace muscle glycogen, the main fuel for exercise, and a suggested post-exercise 'anabolic window' of about 15 to 45 minutes.[1] Bodybuilding sources note that many lifters favour slower-digesting, lower-glycemic carbohydrates for most meals, with faster sugars around workouts.[2]

Sweet potato is popular in this setting as a whole-food starch. Per 100 g, a baked sweet potato in its skin provides about 20.7 g of carbohydrate, 3.3 g of fibre, about 11,500 micrograms of beta-carotene and 475 mg of potassium, according to the USDA-based tables on Wikipedia.[3] The 2017 International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on nutrient timing and a 2013 review by Aragon and Schoenfeld are the main scientific reference points on the topic.[4][5]

Carbohydrate timing sits within the wider idea of nutrient timing, which has a long bodybuilding history and a research literature that has partly revised its claims. In the 2013 Aragon and Schoenfeld review, proponents had claimed timing was more important than total daily intake, and the authors concluded the post-exercise window is probably not as narrow or urgent as often claimed; they suggested focusing on total daily carbohydrate unless an athlete is an endurance competitor or trains several times a day [5].

chain: Eat carbohydrate such as sweet potato around training
Muscle glycogen is available for hard sessions and restored afterwards
Better training output and recovery, supporting muscle gain and a leaner physique
angle.text: Carbohydrate fuels high-intensity training and refills glycogen, so lifters time starchy meals such as sweet potato to the hours around the gym. The appearance payoff comes through training quality and recovery; sweet potato is chosen as a nutrient-dense, whole-food starch.

paras: Proponents say that carbohydrate plus protein around workouts raises glycogen and protein synthesis after training.[1] A common pattern in bodybuilding is to place most starch in the meals before and after the gym, and Wikipedia notes that many lifters favour slower-digesting, lower-glycemic carbohydrates for most meals, with faster sugars around workouts.[2]

For people building or showing off a physique, the practice has an appearance logic: training sessions fuelled by glycogen can be performed at higher intensity and volume, and those sessions are what drive muscle growth, while the same carbohydrates can be placed in the meals that suit a lifter's energy needs during a cut or a bulk. The practice is a way of arranging food rather than adding a new food, and sweet potato is one of several starchy staples used for it, alongside rice, oats and white potato.[1][2][3]

Muscle glycogen is the main fuel at the start of activity, during high-intensity aerobic work and during all anaerobic work, and muscle uses its glycogen only for itself because it cannot release glucose into the blood.[6] Skeletal muscle stores about 1 to 2 percent of its mass as glycogen, roughly 400 g in a 70 kg adult, with the liver holding about 100 to 120 g.[6]

Resistance training draws these stores down. Aragon and Schoenfeld cite a study in which three sets at 80 percent of one-repetition maximum to failure cut muscle glycogen by 24 percent, and another in which six sets at 12 repetitions cut it by 38 percent.[5] They also report that taking carbohydrate straight after exercise speeds resynthesis, and that delaying it by two hours can reduce the rate by up to 50 percent, but that for most lifters the urgency is greatly diminished.[5]

sections.h: Sweet potato as a carbohydrate source
paras: Sweet potato is a staple root that is boiled, baked or roasted, and baking raises maltose from about 10% to 20% of its sugars; carbohydrate is mostly sucrose, starch and fibre, and the orange-fleshed varieties carry the most beta-carotene.[3] It also supplies potassium, with about 16% of the Daily Value per 100 g baked.[3]

On the glycemic index, which scores foods from 0 to 100 by how much they raise blood glucose, Wikipedia lists unpeeled sweet potato as low (55 or less) and peeled sweet potato as medium (56 to 69), compared with 83 for peeled white or yellow potato; cooking and processing can raise a food's score, and the index does not account for portion size, which glycemic load does.[8] Lifters who choose sweet potato commonly cite it as a whole-food source of slower carbohydrate, in line with the bodybuilding preference for lower-glycemic starch most of the day.[2][8]

The 2017 ISSN position stand lists several carbohydrate points: a high-carbohydrate diet of about 8 to 12 g per kg per day maximises glycogen stores; when glycogen must be restored within about four hours, aggressive refeeding at roughly 1.2 g per kg per hour from high-glycemic sources (GI above 70) is suggested; and 30 to 60 g per hour is suggested during high-intensity exercise lasting over about an hour.[4] For resistance exercise it says carbohydrate during training may support blood glucose, glycogen and reduced muscle damage but that results are inconsistent, and in one study carbohydrate reduced glycogen loss without improving performance.[4] The same document stresses meeting total daily protein intake and gives a 20 to 40 g protein bolus as the amount that maximally stimulates muscle protein synthesis.[4]

Aragon and Schoenfeld's 2013 review concluded that the evidence for a narrow, urgent post-workout window is far from definitive, and called carbohydrate timing a gray area without consistent data for firm recommendations.[5] They report that timing of glycogen resynthesis matters mainly for endurance athletes who train again within about 8 hours, that glycogen returns to baseline within 24 hours after resistance training regardless of carbohydrate timing, and that adding carbohydrate to adequate post-exercise protein did not further raise muscle protein balance in the studies cited.[5]

The review notes that the case for post-exercise urgency rests mainly on fasted training, which can leave muscle in a net negative amino acid balance; for lifters training more than about 3 to 4 hours after a meal, it says the classic recommendation of protein soon after training is warranted.[5] Its practical suggestions include keeping pre- and post-exercise meals within about 3 to 4 hours of each other, or up to 5 to 6 hours after a large mixed meal, and prioritising total daily carbohydrate over precise timing except for endurance athletes or those training more than once a day.[5]

Both documents list limitations of the underlying literature: many studies are short-term, measure muscle protein synthesis rather than long-term hypertrophy, enrol small samples of mostly untrained men and confound timing with total protein or energy intake.[4][5] One position-stand author is noted as having a supplement company affiliation.[4]

Pre-event meals of 1 to 4 g per kg several hours before exercise help maintain glycogen, according to the ISSN, though the evidence for carbohydrate in the final hours before exercise is mixed and some athletes experience rebound hypoglycemia that a warm-up or eating closer to the start may reduce.[4] Wikipedia's article on carbohydrate loading says eating carbohydrate within two hours of aerobic exercise can raise insulin and lower blood glucose in susceptible people, which may limit performance in events longer than 60 minutes.[7]

Carbohydrate loading is the endurance-sport relative of carb timing: athletes raise carbohydrate intake in the days before an event to build glycogen, with Wikipedia citing roughly 10 to 12 g per kg for 36 to 48 hours before events over 90 minutes, and noting that about 2.7 g of water is retained per gram of carbohydrate.[7] Starchy foods such as potatoes are among the foods suggested.[7] The ISSN adds that loading combines a brief reduction in training with 8 to 10 g per kg per day.[4]

No studies found on sweet potato specifically for carbohydrate timing. A 2025 crossover trial in 14 resistance-trained men used purple sweet potato as the placebo, not the tested food, when examining red spinach powder before bench press work.[10] Studies of nutrient timing in general exist, including the reviews described above.[4][5]

Carb timing is discussed in lifting forums as one lever among several for a leaner look. A T Nation member recalled that a well-known coach had released material saying that, for a 'carb user', carbohydrate could be timed around workouts, and said they made use of it, with a weekly carbohydrate-heavy meal the night before squat and deadlift sessions.[9] Another member commented on a meal post that a potato-type carbohydrate side could be added next time.[11]

timeline.event: Ivy and Portman publish the book Nutrient Timing.[1]
Aragon and Schoenfeld publish 'Nutrient timing revisited: is there a post-exercise anabolic window?'[5]
International Society of Sports Nutrition publishes its nutrient timing position stand.[4]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding and lifting forums, carbohydrate timing is discussed as a way to fuel training and manage body composition, with sweet potato named as one of several staple starches [9][11].

claims.claim: There is a narrow post-workout 'anabolic window' for carbs
claims.believers: Wikipedia describes a suggested post-exercise window of about 15 to 45 minutes in which carbohydrate and protein are said to replenish glycogen and drive repair [1].
claims.experts: Aragon and Schoenfeld concluded the window is probably not as narrow or urgent as often claimed, and the ISSN says high-quality protein from immediately up to 2 hours after exercise produces robust muscle protein synthesis [5][4].

claims.claim: Carbs should be timed around workouts for 'carb users'
claims.believers: A T Nation member said they used a coach's advice to time carbohydrate around workouts and placed a carbohydrate-heavy meal before squat and deadlift days [9].
claims.experts: The 2013 review suggests prioritising total daily carbohydrate over precise timing unless an athlete trains more than once a day or is an endurance athlete [5].

claims.claim: Slow carbs most of the day and fast carbs around the gym
claims.believers: Bodybuilding sources describe lifters favouring lower-glycemic carbohydrates for most meals and faster sugars around workouts [2].
claims.experts: The ISSN suggests high-glycemic sources (GI above 70) when glycogen must be restored within about four hours, and glycemic index depends on cooking and portion size [4][8].

claims.claim: Sweet potato is a better gym carb than other starches
claims.believers: Lifters cite it as a whole-food source of carbohydrate with beta-carotene and potassium, and unpeeled sweet potato is listed as low glycemic [3][8].
claims.experts: No trial has tested sweet potato against other carbohydrate sources for timing, and the reviews discuss carbohydrate in general terms [4][5].

claims.claim: Glycogen is refilled quickly if you eat carbs after training
claims.believers: Proponents say carbohydrate after workouts restores muscle glycogen, the main fuel for exercise [1].
claims.experts: Delaying carbohydrate by two hours can reduce resynthesis rate by up to 50 percent, but glycogen returns to baseline within 24 hours after resistance training regardless of timing [5].

claims.claim: Carbs eaten before training always help performance
claims.believers: Pre-workout carbohydrate is described as fuel for harder training [1].
claims.experts: The ISSN reports mixed evidence for carbohydrate in the final hours before exercise, with rebound hypoglycemia in some athletes, and inconsistent results in resistance training [4][7].
